questions.q: When is foreach the right loop to reach for?
options: When you already have a collection — like a list of servers — and want to do the same thing to each item
When you have no idea how many times the loop should run
When you only need to count from 1 to a fixed number with no other data
foreach can only be used with numbers, never strings
questions.explain: foreach iterates over a collection you already have in a variable.

questions.q: How does foreach differ from ForEach-Object, covered in Lesson 8?
options: foreach is a language keyword operating on a collection already in a variable, while ForEach-Object receives items one at a time from the pipeline
They are exactly identical in every way with no functional difference
ForEach-Object can only be used inside a while loop
foreach is deprecated and should never be used
questions.explain: Both loop over items, but foreach works on an existing collection variable while ForEach-Object works mid-pipeline.

questions.q: Why is while the right tool for a connection retry loop?
options: while doesn't need to know the iteration count in advance — it keeps going as long as its condition stays true, which fits waiting for success
while always runs exactly 5 times no matter what
while can only be used with string comparisons
while is identical to for in every situation
questions.explain: while is condition-based, not collection-based or count-based, which matches an unknown number of retry attempts.

questions.q: What are the three parts inside a for loop's parentheses?
options: A starting value, a condition checked before each pass, and what happens after each pass (like an increment)
Three unrelated variable names with no connection to each other
A collection, a filter, and a sort order
for loops in PowerShell don't use parentheses at all
questions.explain: for ($i = 1; $i -le 5; $i++) shows the standard shape: start, condition, increment.

questions.q: According to the lesson, why shouldn't these three loop types be treated as interchangeable?
options: Each answers a different question — a collection you have, a condition to wait on, or a count to control — and forcing the wrong one means hand-rolling logic the right loop already provides
PowerShell technically disallows using the wrong loop type and throws a syntax error
Only foreach is valid inside a function
while and for produce different data types as output
questions.explain: The lesson frames the choice as matching the loop to what you actually have on hand, not personal preference.
